title: The Waiter Who Forgot the Bill

lines.text: A Berlin waiter forgot his table's orders once they'd paid.
The story goes that the psychologist Kurt Lewin was dining there.
lines.say: The story goes that the psychologist Koort Leh-veen was dining there.

lines.text: About half an hour later, Lewin asked him to write the bill out again.
lines.say: About half an hour later, Leh-veen asked him to write the bill out again.

lines.text: He no longer knew. While the bill was open, he seemed to hold every detail. Once it was settled, it was gone.
Bluma Zeigarnik, who worked with Lewin, put it to the test.
lines.say: Bloo-mah Zay-gar-nik, who worked with Leh-veen, put it to the test.

lines.text: Thirty-two adults worked through a run of small tasks.
She let them finish half, and stopped the rest when they were most absorbed.
They recalled the interrupted tasks almost twice as well as the finished ones.
She published in 1927, and it became known as the Zeigarnik effect.
lines.say: She published in nineteen twenty-seven, and it became known as the Zay-gar-nik effect.

lines.text: The idea: an unfinished task stays active in the mind.
It has proved harder to show than the waiter's story suggests.
Her name now turns up wherever people talk about cliffhangers and nagging to-do lists.

caption: A waiter who forgot a paid bill led to the Zeigarnik effect, the idea that unfinished tasks stick in the mind. It has proved harder to show than the story suggests. A true story, fact-checked. Curiouser No. 9
